title: Docker basics
intro: Docker gives you a consistent way to package and run applications together with the environment they need. In this lesson, you will learn the core Docker concepts and commands, build a production-oriented image for a Spring Boot application, and see how a Vite React frontend can be served efficiently with nginx.
body:
## Why Docker matters

When an application works on your machine but fails somewhere else, the problem is often not the application code itself. Different Java versions, operating system packages, environment variables, file paths, or installed tools can produce different behaviour.

Docker addresses this by packaging an application into a **container image** that describes the environment needed to run it. A container created from that image then runs in an isolated environment with predictable dependencies.

Docker does not replace your application or your server. It gives you a standard way to package, start, inspect, and stop applications.

For the project you have been building, a typical deployment might eventually look like this:

~~~text
React frontend -> nginx container
                    |
                    v
             Spring Boot container
                    |
                    v
             PostgreSQL container
~~~

Each part can be packaged and deployed independently.

---

## Images and containers

An **image** is a packaged, immutable description of an application environment. It contains the files, libraries, runtime, and instructions needed to create a container.

~~~diagram
{"type": "flow", "title": "Image vs. container", "caption": "An image is a read-only template; every container is a running instance with its own writable layer.", "nodes": [{"id": "df", "label": "Dockerfile", "kind": "file"}, {"id": "img", "label": "Image", "sub": "shop-api:1.4", "kind": "file", "highlight": true}, {"id": "reg", "label": "Registry", "sub": "ghcr.io", "kind": "cloud"}, {"id": "c1", "label": "Container 1", "sub": "running", "kind": "server"}, {"id": "c2", "label": "Container 2", "sub": "running", "kind": "server"}], "edges": [{"from": "df", "to": "img", "label": "docker build"}, {"from": "img", "to": "reg", "label": "docker push"}, {"from": "img", "to": "c1", "label": "docker run"}, {"from": "img", "to": "c2", "label": "docker run"}]}
~~~

A **container** is a running instance of an image.

A useful mental model is:

~~~text
Docker image = blueprint
Docker container = running instance of the blueprint
~~~

For example, you might build an image called `task-api:1.0`. You can then start several containers from the same image.

~~~text
docker build -t task-api:1.0 .
docker run --name task-api task-api:1.0
~~~

The image itself does not normally change when the container starts. The container gets its own writable layer on top of the image.

You can therefore build an image once and run it in development, testing, staging, and production environments, while providing environment-specific configuration through environment variables or other deployment configuration.

---

## Layers and the Docker build cache

Docker images are built in **layers**. Many Dockerfile instructions create a layer or contribute to the final image filesystem.

~~~widget docker-layers
~~~

This matters because Docker can reuse previously built layers when the relevant inputs have not changed.

Consider this simplified Dockerfile:

~~~dockerfile
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jdk
WORKDIR /app
COPY pom.xml .
RUN ./mvnw dependency:go-offline
COPY src ./src
RUN ./mvnw package -DskipTests
~~~

The expensive dependency-related step can potentially be reused when only application source code changes. If you instead copy the entire project before every build step, small source changes can invalidate more of the cache.

Caching is therefore both a performance feature and a reason to think about the order of Dockerfile instructions.

You should not treat the cache as a correctness mechanism. A build must still produce the correct image when the cache is unavailable. The cache only makes repeated builds faster.

---

## A multi-stage Dockerfile for Spring Boot

A Spring Boot application built with Maven produces a JAR file. You could create an image containing the full JDK and your source tree, but that is usually unnecessary for production.

~~~diagram
{"type": "flow", "title": "Multi-stage build", "nodes": [{"id": "b", "label": "Stage 1: build", "sub": "temurin:21-jdk + Maven ≈ 500 MB", "kind": "code"}, {"id": "jar", "label": "app.jar", "kind": "file", "highlight": true}, {"id": "r", "label": "Stage 2: runtime", "sub": "temurin:21-jre ≈ 200 MB", "kind": "server", "highlight": true}, {"id": "x", "label": "Discarded", "sub": "JDK, sources, ~/.m2"}], "edges": [{"from": "b", "to": "jar", "label": "mvn package"}, {"from": "jar", "to": "r", "label": "COPY --from=build"}, {"from": "b", "to": "x", "dashed": true}]}
~~~

A **multi-stage build** lets you use one image for building and another, smaller image for running the application.

For a Java 21 Spring Boot application, a practical Dockerfile can look like this:

~~~dockerfile
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jdk AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY . .
RUN ./mvnw -q package -DskipTests

FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build /app/target/task-api.jar app.jar
RUN useradd --system appuser
USER appuser
EXPOSE 8080
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "app.jar"]
~~~

The first stage contains the JDK because Maven needs the Java development tools to compile the application.

The second stage contains only the JRE runtime. The compiled application is copied from the build stage with `COPY --from=build`.

This has several benefits:

- The final image does not need your Maven build environment.
- The final image does not need your source code.
- The runtime image can be smaller than the JDK-based build image.
- The separation makes the purpose of each stage clear.

The `./mvnw` command uses the Maven Wrapper included in the project. This is useful because the project controls the Maven version rather than depending on whatever Maven version happens to be installed on the host.

The `-DskipTests` option is often used when producing the deployment artifact in this simple example. In a real CI/CD pipeline, tests should normally run as a separate earlier step, so a broken application does not get packaged and deployed.

---

## Running as a non-root user

A container process should not normally run as the root user when it does not need root privileges.

This Dockerfile creates a system user and switches to it:

~~~dockerfile
RUN useradd --system appuser
USER appuser
~~~

The important detail is that `USER appuser` comes after the user has been created. From that point onward, the application runs as that user.

Running as a non-root user reduces the impact of some security problems. If an attacker manages to exploit a vulnerability in the application, the process does not automatically have root privileges inside the container.

This is one of those small deployment decisions that is easy to overlook when an application is still running only on a developer laptop.

---

## EXPOSE and port mapping

`EXPOSE` documents the port the application listens on inside the container:

~~~callout info EXPOSE does not publish a port
`EXPOSE 8080` is documentation. The port only becomes reachable from your machine with `-p 8080:8080` (host:container) on `docker run`, or `ports:` in Compose.
~~~

~~~dockerfile
EXPOSE 8080
~~~

It does **not** publish the port to your host automatically.

To make a container port accessible from your machine, use `-p` with `docker run`:

~~~text
docker run --name task-api -p 8080:8080 task-api:1.0
~~~

The format is:

~~~text
-p host-port:container-port
~~~

So `8080:8080` means that requests to port 8080 on the host are forwarded to port 8080 inside the container.

The two numbers do not have to be identical. For example:

~~~text
docker run --name task-api -p 9000:8080 task-api:1.0
~~~

Now you access the application through port 9000 on the host while the application still listens on 8080 inside the container.

This distinction becomes particularly useful when several containers expose similar internal ports.

---

## ENTRYPOINT

The `ENTRYPOINT` defines the main process that should run when the container starts.

For Spring Boot:

~~~dockerfile
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "app.jar"]
~~~

This is the JSON/exec form of `ENTRYPOINT`. Docker starts Java directly rather than passing the command through a shell.

You can now build and run the image:

~~~text
docker build -t task-api:1.0 .
docker run --name task-api -p 8080:8080 task-api:1.0
~~~

If the application starts correctly, it should be available at port 8080 on your host.

---

## The .dockerignore file

The Docker build context is the directory you provide to `docker build`. If you run:

~~~text
docker build -t task-api .
~~~

then `.` is the build context.

You usually do not want to send everything in the project directory to Docker. Create a `.dockerignore` file to exclude unnecessary files:

~~~text
.git
.idea
node_modules
target
*.log
.env
~~~

The exact list depends on the project. The important principle is to keep the build context small and avoid accidentally copying development-only files or secrets.

Never use `.dockerignore` as your only secret-management mechanism. A secret that was copied into an image layer can remain in image history even if a later layer removes the file. Secrets should be provided through appropriate environment or secret-management mechanisms.

---

## Essential Docker commands

You do not need hundreds of Docker commands to start working effectively. A small set covers most everyday tasks.

### Build an image

~~~text
docker build -t task-api:1.0 .
~~~

`-t` assigns a name and optionally a tag to the image.

### Start a container

~~~text
docker run --name task-api -p 8080:8080 task-api:1.0
~~~

To run it in the background, use detached mode:

~~~text
docker run -d --name task-api -p 8080:8080 task-api:1.0
~~~

### List running containers

~~~text
docker ps
~~~

To include stopped containers:

~~~text
docker ps -a
~~~

### Read logs

~~~text
docker logs task-api
~~~

Logs are often the first place to look when a container starts and immediately stops or an application fails during startup.

### Execute a command inside a running container

~~~text
docker exec -it task-api sh
~~~

This opens a shell inside the container when the image provides one. It is useful for debugging, but it should not become a substitute for proper application logging and observability.

### Stop a container

~~~text
docker stop task-api
~~~

These commands form a useful basic workflow:

~~~text
build -> run -> ps -> logs -> exec -> stop
~~~

---

## Environment variables

Applications should not hard-code environment-specific configuration into the image.

For example, your Spring Boot application might read a database URL from an environment variable. You can provide it when starting the container:

~~~text
docker run -d \
  --name task-api \
  -p 8080:8080 \
  -e SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL=jdbc:postgresql://db:5432/tasks \
  task-api:1.0
~~~

The image remains the same while the configuration changes between environments.

You can also provide several variables:

~~~text
docker run -d \
  --name task-api \
  -e SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod \
  -e APP_FEATURE_X=true \
  task-api:1.0
~~~

Do not put passwords, API keys, or other secrets directly into a Dockerfile. Treat environment variables carefully as well: depending on the platform and configuration, they may be visible to people or systems with access to the container configuration.

---

## Dockerizing a Vite React frontend

A Vite React application also benefits from a multi-stage build. The development environment needs Node.js to install dependencies and build the application, but the browser only needs the generated static files.

A typical Dockerfile can use Node for the build stage and nginx for the runtime stage:

~~~dockerfile
FROM node:22 AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build

FROM nginx:alpine
COPY --from=build /app/dist /usr/share/nginx/html
EXPOSE 80
CMD ["nginx", "-g", "daemon off;"]
~~~

The first stage creates the Vite production build. The second stage serves the generated static files with nginx.

This is a common deployment pattern for React applications because the production browser does not need Node.js, npm, TypeScript, or the source files.

For a client-side router, such as React Router, nginx may also need configuration that falls back to `index.html` for application routes. Otherwise, directly opening a route such as `/tasks/42` can result in a 404 from nginx even though the React application itself knows that route.

---

## Docker Desktop and IntelliJ IDEA

On a developer machine, **Docker Desktop** provides Docker Engine and a convenient graphical interface. On macOS and Windows, it is commonly used to run Linux containers locally.

After Docker Desktop is running, IntelliJ IDEA Community Edition can be used alongside Docker for your development workflow. Depending on the IntelliJ IDEA version and installed plugins, Docker-related integration can expose containers, images, logs, and other resources through the **Services** tool window.

The graphical interface is convenient, but learning the CLI is still important. The same Docker concepts and commands are used in CI/CD environments and remote servers where you may not have a graphical interface.

A good workflow is therefore to understand the commands first and use IntelliJ's Services window as a convenient visual representation of what Docker is doing.

---

## Common mistakes

### Treating an image and a container as the same thing

An image is the package; a container is an instance running from that package. Rebuilding an image and restarting an existing container are different operations.

### Assuming EXPOSE publishes a port

`EXPOSE 8080` documents the container port. You still need `-p 8080:8080` when you want to publish it to the host.

### Copying unnecessary files

A large build context slows builds and can accidentally include files that should never enter the image. Use `.dockerignore`.

### Running the application as root

If the application does not require root privileges, create a dedicated user and use `USER` in the final image.

### Putting secrets into the Dockerfile

Dockerfiles can be inspected and image layers can persist. Keep credentials and other secrets outside the image.

### Using fixed sleep commands for startup

A container being started does not necessarily mean that the application inside it is ready. When containers depend on each other, use proper health checks, retries, or application-level readiness mechanisms rather than arbitrary delays.

### Making every container a development environment

A production image should contain what is required to run the application, not every tool you use while developing it. Multi-stage builds help separate those concerns.

---

## A practical deployment workflow

For the task manager application, a simple container workflow might look like this:

~~~text
1. Run tests in CI
2. Build the Spring Boot JAR
3. Build the Spring Boot Docker image
4. Build the React production bundle
5. Build the nginx Docker image
6. Start the containers with environment-specific configuration
7. Verify logs and health
8. Publish the images to a registry
9. Deploy the images to the target server
~~~

Docker is not the entire DevOps process. It is one important building block that makes the application artifact portable and repeatable.

Once you understand images, containers, Dockerfiles, networking, environment variables, and basic lifecycle commands, the next step is connecting those pieces to automated CI/CD and a real deployment environment.

The goal is not to memorise every Docker command. The goal is to understand what is being packaged, where it runs, how it receives configuration, and how you can inspect it when something goes wrong.
takeaways: An image is a packaged application environment, while a container is a running instance of that image.
Docker layers and build caching make repeated image builds faster when Dockerfile instructions are structured well.
Multi-stage Dockerfiles keep build dependencies out of the final Spring Boot runtime image.
EXPOSE documents a container port, while -p maps a host port to that container port.
Production containers should avoid unnecessary files, secrets, and root privileges.
A React production build can be served efficiently from a small nginx runtime image.

quiz.question: What is the main difference between a Docker image and a Docker container?
options: An image is a running process, while a container is a Dockerfile
An image is a packaged environment, while a container is a running instance of that image
An image is always smaller than a container
A container can only be created without an image
quiz.explanation: An image is the immutable package used to create containers. A container is a running or stopped instance created from an image.

quiz.question: Why is a multi-stage Dockerfile useful for a Spring Boot application?
options: It allows the build stage to use the JDK while the final image only needs the runtime
It makes Docker containers run without an operating system
It automatically creates a PostgreSQL database
It prevents Docker from using build caching
quiz.explanation: The build stage can contain the JDK and build tools, while the final stage can contain only the JRE and application JAR, producing a cleaner runtime image.

quiz.question: What does `-p 9000:8080` mean in `docker run`?
options: The container uses port 9000 and the host uses port 8080
Docker changes the application's internal port from 8080 to 9000
Host port 9000 is mapped to container port 8080
The container exposes both ports automatically
quiz.explanation: The port mapping format is host-port:container-port. Therefore, requests sent to port 9000 on the host are forwarded to port 8080 in the container.

quiz.question: Which Dockerfile instruction switches the application process to a previously created non-root user?
options: RUN
EXPOSE
COPY
USER
quiz.explanation: USER changes the user that subsequent Dockerfile instructions and the container's main process run as.

quiz.question: Why is nginx commonly used as the runtime image for a production Vite React frontend?
options: It compiles TypeScript inside the browser
It can efficiently serve the generated static files without requiring Node.js at runtime
It replaces React Router automatically
It stores the application's PostgreSQL database
quiz.explanation: After Vite builds the React application, the result is static HTML, JavaScript, CSS, and assets. nginx can serve those files without Node.js or npm.

exercise.title: Generate Docker commands and a Spring Boot Dockerfile
exercise.task:
Define exactly these two functions:

1. `function buildDockerfile(opts: { javaVersion: number; jarName: string; port: number }): string` — return a multi-stage Dockerfile as lines joined with `"\n"`. The returned string must contain these lines in exactly this order, although other lines are allowed in between:
   - `FROM eclipse-temurin:<javaVersion>-jdk AS build`
   - `WORKDIR /app`
   - `COPY . .`
   - `RUN ./mvnw -q package -DskipTests`
   - `FROM eclipse-temurin:<javaVersion>-jre`
   - `WORKDIR /app`
   - `COPY --from=build /app/target/<jarName> app.jar`
   - `RUN useradd --system appuser`
   - `USER appuser`
   - `EXPOSE <port>`
   - `ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "app.jar"]`

2. `function dockerRun(opts: { image: string; name: string; ports?: [number, number][]; env?: Record<string, string>; detach?: boolean }): string` — return `"docker run"`, followed by `"-d"` when `detach` is true, then `"--name <name>"`, then one `"-p host:container"` argument for each port pair, then one `"-e KEY=value"` argument for each environment variable in insertion order, and finally the image. Join every part with a single space.

The functions should work for different Java versions, JAR names, ports, images, names, port mappings, and environment variables. Do not hard-code the values from a single example.
exercise.hint: For `buildDockerfile`, construct an array of Dockerfile lines and use `join("\n")` at the end. Interpolate `javaVersion`, `jarName`, and `port` into the required lines. For `dockerRun`, build an array of command parts, conditionally add `-d`, add the name, iterate over ports and environment entries in their natural insertion order, add the image last, and join the parts with a single space.

tests.name: It keeps the required Dockerfile lines in order
It substitutes the Java version in both FROM lines
It substitutes the JAR name in the COPY line
tests.code:
const result = buildDockerfile({ javaVersion: 21, jarName: "orders-service-1.2.3.jar", port: 8080 });
return result.split("\n").includes("COPY --from=build /app/target/orders-service-1.2.3.jar app.jar");

tests.name: It places USER after useradd
It exposes the requested port
tests.code:
const result = buildDockerfile({ javaVersion: 21, jarName: "app.jar", port: 9090 });
return result.split("\n").includes("EXPOSE 9090");

tests.name: It uses the exact Java ENTRYPOINT
tests.code:
const result = buildDockerfile({ javaVersion: 21, jarName: "app.jar", port: 8080 });
return result.split("\n").includes('ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "app.jar"]');

tests.name: It adds detach mode when requested
tests.code:
const result = dockerRun({ image: "task-api:1.0", name: "task-api", detach: true });
return result === "docker run -d --name task-api task-api:1.0";

tests.name: It omits detach mode when not requested
tests.code:
const result = dockerRun({ image: "task-api:1.0", name: "task-api" });
return result === "docker run --name task-api task-api:1.0";

tests.name: It preserves multiple ports and environment variable order
It has no double spaces when ports and environment variables are missing
tests.code:
const result = dockerRun({ image: "frontend:1.0", name: "frontend" });
return result === "docker run --name frontend frontend:1.0" && !result.includes("  ");
